section_summary: This section follows American and British oil companies as they negotiate with Japanese officials and Mitsui over mandatory petroleum stocks, storage costs, sales quotas, and assurances about their future trade in Japan. It also covers coal hydrogenation, Japanese fuel policy, and a Japanese oil concession in Mexico. By December 1936, the companies considered the government’s written assurances inadequate, prompting discussion of coordinated American and British diplomatic representations.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed arrangement under which Mitsui would hold the foreign companies’ mandatory oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: Company representatives proposed that Mitsui carry noncommercial stocks in return for government compensation and a share of their Japanese business. Yoshino welcomed continued foreign operations, but no final agreement had been reached.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on petroleum law developments
subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo despatch No. 1914 and the revised stockholding assurance submitted by foreign oil companies.
subfiles.summary: Japanese authorities required a prompt written assurance before granting continued sales quotas. The companies submitted a revised statement that appeared acceptable, while their principals accepted Mitsui’s proposal in principle.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan, despatch No. 1914
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports negotiations over the foreign companies’ stockholding declaration and Mitsui’s storage proposal.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials sought an unequivocal promise to meet the Petroleum Industry Law’s stockholding requirement and warned that sales quotas could suffer without one. After Yoshino suggested softer wording, the companies submitted a statement that they were negotiating an arrangement and had reached agreement in principle. Their principals also accepted Mitsui’s proposal in principle, subject to details.

subfiles.title: Notes of interview at Department of Commerce and Industry, June 13
subfiles.about: Records Sakai’s discussion with Meyer, Ely, and Ezoye about proposed Japanese storage of foreign oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: Company representatives described negotiations with Japanese interests to provide mandatory stocks and storage. Sakai warned that the ministry might act against the companies if progress remained uncertain, and discussed how the issue applied in Korea and Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Notes of interview at Department of Commerce and Industry, June 22
subfiles.about: Records Kojima’s demand for a firm written stockholding commitment.
subfiles.summary: Kojima insisted that the companies declare they would fulfill the law’s stockholding requirement; Meyer and Ely resisted wording that separated that promise from the special arrangement they needed.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding despatch No. 1914 to London
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew’s June 26 despatch on the oil situation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sends despatch No. 1914 and its enclosures for the ambassador’s information.

subfiles.title: Bureau of Mines letter on hydrogenation references
subfiles.from: J. S. McGrath, Bureau of Mines
subfiles.about: Provides technical literature references requested by the American Consulate at Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau points the consulate to periodical articles and the 1933 World Petroleum Congress proceedings on petroleum and coal hydrogenation, and offers to seek photostat copies if needed.

subfiles.title: Jap Oil Law: U.S. Unit Accepts
subfiles.about: Reports that Standard-Vacuum and Rising Sun accepted the oil law’s storage provisions.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reports a compromise over six months’ oil storage while tank facilities remained unavailable.

subfiles.title: Japanese Quota Action Pleases U.S. Oil Firms
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan maintained foreign companies’ sales quotas despite unresolved excess stocks.
subfiles.summary: Company officials welcomed unchanged quotas but remained concerned that the allotments gave them no share of rising demand.

subfiles.title: Parker letter on quotas, storage company, and hydrogenation
subfiles.about: Updates the State Department on quotas and a joint American-British storage proposal.
subfiles.summary: Parker reports unchanged quarterly quotas, negotiations for a Japanese storage company, and an offer of hydrogenation processes that might aid the talks.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledgment of Parker’s letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Parker’s July 14 report on the Japanese oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton welcomes the unchanged quotas and asks Parker to continue reporting developments.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Division of Far Eastern Affairs note
subfiles.about: Comments on a despatch concerning progress toward resolving foreign oil interests’ difficulties.
subfiles.summary: Notes progress toward settlement and urges reading the despatch in full.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan, despatch No. 1938
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports maintained quotas, talks with Yoshino and Mitsui, and a proposed coal hydrogenation sale.
subfiles.summary: The companies obtained July–September quotas at earlier levels after submitting a statement about future storage, though they received no share of increased demand. Yoshino said the Five Point Memorandum’s benefits would apply once stockholding obligations were met. Mitsui discussions settled several tank and stock handling points, while company representatives also considered selling the I.G. coal hydrogenation process.

subfiles.title: Notes of conversation with Yoshino, July 4
subfiles.about: Records Yoshino’s explanations of press reports and assurances about future foreign oil quotas.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino said press accounts had overstated the companies’ acceptance of stockholding obligations. He affirmed the Five Point Memorandum’s principles and said the companies could share fairly in increased consumption after meeting the law, while noting unresolved questions for Korea and Taiwan.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding despatch No. 1938 to London
subfiles.about: Forwards the July 10 despatch on oil interests in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sends despatch No. 1938 and its enclosure for information.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Japanese oil concessions in Mexico
subfiles.about: Points to a letter and memorandum about a Japanese company organized to operate in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Parker’s material concerning Sanchu Ikeda’s Japanese oil venture in Mexico.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan, despatch No. 1977
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Mitsui negotiations, Japanese pressure for storage, hydrogenation plans, and an oil concession in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui and the foreign companies had agreed in principle but still disputed storage limits and compensation; the companies projected tank construction by September and oil storage around April 1937. Grew also reports an offer to sell the I.G. coal hydrogenation process, Japanese plans for a process pool, and a Japanese company’s Tehuantepec Valley concession.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on despatches Nos. 1977 and 1989
subfiles.about: Summarizes slow storage negotiations and Japanese efforts to expand domestic fuel supplies.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes official impatience with Mitsui negotiations and reviews proposals for coal hydrogenation and alcohol blended with gasoline. It highlights the Embassy’s view that Japan might eventually gain a substantial measure of fuel independence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1989 on American oil interests and national fuel policy
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the pace of Mitsui negotiations and emerging Japanese national fuel proposals.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui talks moved slowly because both sides referred points to their head offices, and Yoshino warned that the government might intervene. The despatch surveys plans for a fuel bureau, coal liquefaction in Manchuria, higher gasoline prices, and possible alcohol blending. Grew weighs the difficulty of fuel independence against Japan’s record in developing other industries.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding despatches Nos. 1977 and 1989 to London
subfiles.about: Forwards two Tokyo despatches on the Japanese oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Sends the August 6 and August 20 despatches for information.

subfiles.title: Document file note for despatch No. 1991
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on the Petroleum Industry Law and American oil interests.
subfiles.summary: Points to despatch No. 1991 in another file.

subfiles.title: Relations with the United States: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes July negotiations by Standard-Vacuum and Rising Sun with Japanese officials and Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: Reports apparent agreement in principle with both the authorities and Mitsui.

subfiles.title: Document file note for despatch No. 2046
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report on the companies’ planned storage tank construction.
subfiles.summary: Points to a report that tank construction was to begin by September’s end.

subfiles.title: Relations with the United States: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes storage plans and unresolved compensation questions.
subfiles.summary: The companies projected tank construction by September 1936 and storage by April 1937, while seeking firm limits and compensation terms.

subfiles.title: Parker letter reporting agreement in principle
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese acceptance in principle of a Mitsui storage arrangement.
subfiles.summary: Parker says Mitsui would build tanks and buy stocks, receiving a government subsidy and commissions on business ceded by the foreign companies.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply to Parker
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Parker’s account of progress toward a Mitsui agreement.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck welcomes the prospect of an early settlement and Parker’s appreciation of Embassy and Department assistance.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Parker’s letter to Tokyo
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends Parker’s October 20 letter to the Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Parker’s update and his appreciation for the Embassy’s assistance.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on despatch No. 2076
subfiles.about: Draws attention to a despatch on Mitsui negotiations and oral Japanese assurances.
subfiles.summary: Recommends reading the despatch in full for its account of the oral agreement and assurances.

subfiles.title: American Oil Interests in Japan, despatch No. 2076
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Details the provisional Mitsui storage bargain and Japanese government assurances sought by the foreign companies.
subfiles.summary: After prolonged bargaining, Mitsui and the foreign companies reached a verbal arrangement for Mitsui to invest about ¥17 million in tanks and stocks, with a 7.5 percent annual return funded by government compensation and marketing commissions. Japanese officials gave oral assurances on compensation, quotas, and prices, but a stockholding ceiling remained uncertain. The companies requested written confirmation; the Embassy proposed seeking additional confirmation through the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Telegram approving request for confirmation of assurances
subfiles.about: Approves the Embassy’s proposed approach for confirming Japanese assurances.
subfiles.summary: The Department approves the approach and suggests seeking written confirmation if feasible.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding despatch No. 2076 to London
subfiles.about: Forwards the October 14 Tokyo despatch on the oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Sends despatch No. 2076 for the ambassador’s information.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram No. 259 on impasse over written assurances
subfiles.about: Urges diplomatic action after Japan fails to confirm assurances in satisfactory written form.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports company concern over weak written assurances, reduced kerosene quotas, and a proposed tariff revision. His British colleague favors representations in London; Grew recommends a parallel American conversation with Saito in Washington.

subfiles.title: Telegram to London on proposed diplomatic approach
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s preference for approaches to the Japanese prime minister in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The Department favors coordinated conversations by the American and British ambassadors in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Corrected copy of Grew telegram No. 261
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese oil companies’ opposition to higher foreign gasoline quotas.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays an Asahi report that domestic companies opposed quota increases because foreign firms had not met storage obligations.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram No. 261
subfiles.about: Transmits the Asahi report on opposition to foreign gasoline quota increases.
subfiles.summary: A second copy of the report on domestic oil companies’ opposition to higher foreign quotas.

subfiles.title: Department telegram No. 160 on coordinated representations
subfiles.about: Authorizes coordinated American and British approaches to the Japanese prime minister.
subfiles.summary: After hearing from Standard-Vacuum’s Coe, the Department agrees that diplomatic representations are warranted. It asks Grew to coordinate with his British colleague on nearly simultaneous approaches in Tokyo, expressing concern for the companies’ future and requesting clear written assurances.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Kersey F. Coe
subfiles.about: Records State Department discussion of the oil negotiation impasse and possible diplomatic representations.
subfiles.summary: Coe described Standard-Vacuum’s doubts about Japanese good faith and requested diplomatic action. Participants agreed that coordinated conversations with Japan’s prime minister in Tokyo would be most useful, seeking assurance that the companies could remain and written confirmation of earlier promises.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum memorandum on the petroleum negotiations
subfiles.from: Kersey F. Coe, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Sets out the company’s objections to Japan’s written response, proposed tariff, and kerosene quotas.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews the 1935 Five Point Memorandum and the subsequent Mitsui storage arrangement. Standard-Vacuum argues that Japan’s November reply falls short of an unqualified affirmation and that proposed tariff changes and kerosene quota allocations discriminate against importers.

subfiles.title: Japan Petroleum Control Law: Five Point Memorandum
subfiles.about: Lists understandings on gallonage, future quotas, stocks, gasoline prices, and discrimination.
subfiles.summary: Records the five undertakings cited by the foreign oil companies in their dispute with Japan.

subfiles.title: Incoming cablegram from P. W. Parker
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s unsatisfactory response to requests for assurances and details a kerosene quota complaint.
subfiles.summary: Parker says the government’s reply was ambiguous, Embassy staff agreed it was inadequate, and the Mining Bureau’s kerosene allocations had harmed Standard-Vacuum. The cablegram continues beyond this section.
